title: A stopping voltage is a magnitude with a sign convention
question: Why does retarding an electron not make its charge positive?
recap: The ideal stopping-potential magnitude is Kmax divided by the positive elementary-charge magnitude. Partial transfer or internal losses produce an inequality rather than a larger endpoint energy.
premises: e denotes a positive charge magnitude; the electron charge is −e.
A retarding potential removes kinetic energy, with the sign convention of the electrodes stated.
limitations: No stopping endpoint for emitted electrons is supplied when emission is not allowed.
A negative energy deficit and a signed collector voltage are different quantities.
The footnote gives no size for the work of freeing an electron from a molecule; the passage's figures for it are hypothetical.

overview.text: The ideal stopping-potential magnitude is Kmax divided by the positive elementary-charge magnitude. Partial transfer or internal losses produce an inequality rather than a larger endpoint energy.

full.spoken: The positive charge magnitude times the stopping-voltage magnitude equals maximum kinetic energy, h frequency minus escape work.

full.text: \(V_s\) is a nonnegative magnitude. The sign of a laboratory electrode voltage must also specify which electrode is the reference. Using \(e\) for a positive magnitude does not change the negative charge of the electron.

If the electron receives only part of the available energy or loses energy inside matter, its outgoing kinetic energy is at most \(h\nu - \Phi\). These losses do not reverse the frequency dependence or turn extra intensity into extra energy for one electron.

A footnote to the stopping condition allows that the light may also have to free each electron from a neutral molecule, at the cost of some work, before the electron can leave. The paper says nothing in the derived relation changes: its \(P'\), which it defines as the potential of a gram-equivalent of negative electricity with respect to the body, is then read as a sum of two terms, the work to free the electron and the work to leave the body. In the letters used here, \(\Phi\) stands for that sum, and the stopping potential still rises in a straight line with frequency, with the same slope.

An inverse energy-budget question asks for the smallest accelerating-potential magnitude capable of supplying a quantum \(h\nu\). Within that idealized conversion, \(eV\) must be at least \(h\nu\). This is an energetic lower bound, not a promise that every collision produces light.

full.returnCaption: Return to charge magnitude, signed voltage, and the retarding energy budget.
Return to the stopping voltage, beside the paper's 4.3-volt check in electromagnetic units.

steps.text: Letters: the paper charges the illuminated body to a positive potential Π and writes ε for the electron's charge. This explanation writes \(V_s\) for the size of the stopping potential and e for the positive size of the electron's charge; the electron's charge itself is −e.

items: Set the arrangement and the sign: the body is at the potential \(V_s\) above the conductors around it, which are at zero. An electron leaving the body is pulled back toward it, so the potential retards the electron.

An electron moving from the body out to the surroundings, across a potential difference \(V_s\), loses kinetic energy \(eV_s\). If it had kinetic energy K at the surface, it arrives with \(K-eV_s\), or is turned back if that would be negative.
The body stops losing electricity when even the fastest electron is turned back, that is, when \(eV_s\) equals the largest kinetic energy \(K_{\mathrm{max}}\).
Insert the one-quantum budget of the previous passage for \(K_{\mathrm{max}}\).

steps.spoken: The positive charge magnitude times the stopping-voltage magnitude equals maximum kinetic energy, h frequency minus escape work.

items: Divide by e: \(V_s=(h\nu-\Phi)/e\). Worked with the previous passage's hypothetical numbers: \(K_{\mathrm{max}}\) is 0.4814 electron volts, so \(V_s\) is 0.4814 volts, since one electron volt is e times one volt.

Keep sizes and signs apart. \(V_s\) is a size, zero or positive. The electron's charge is negative, and writing e for its size does not change that. A voltage read from an instrument also needs its reference electrode named.

The paper's gram-equivalent form of the stopping condition is \(ΠE=R\beta\nu-P'\), with \(P'\) the potential of a gram-equivalent of negative electricity with respect to the body: the work for that much electricity to leave it. A footnote attached to it takes up one more possibility.

Suppose the light must first free each electron from a neutral molecule, at the cost of a certain work, before the electron can make its way out. The footnote says nothing in the derived relation changes; \(P'\) is then to be read as a sum of two terms.

Why nothing changes: one quantum's energy, (R/N)βν per electron (\(h\nu\) in the explanatory letters), now pays two works in turn, freeing the electron from its molecule and taking it out of the body. Both come out of the same quantum, so the fastest electron keeps the quantum's energy less their sum. Write \(\Phi\) for the sum, and \(eV_s=h\nu-\Phi\) stands as before.

Worked case, with hypothetical numbers: freeing the electron costs 1.0 electron volt and leaving the body 2.0, so \(\Phi\) is 3.0 electron volts. A quantum of 3.5 electron volts leaves the fastest electron 3.5 − 1.0 − 2.0 = 0.5 electron volts, and \(V_s\) is 0.5 volts. A quantum of 2.5 electron volts releases no electron from the body.

What stays: the frequency enters only through the quantum's energy, so the stopping potential plotted against frequency is still a straight line whose slope does not depend on the substance. The two works together only move the frequency at which the line reaches zero.

Partial transfer and losses: if an electron receives only part of a quantum, or loses energy inside the body, it reaches the surface with less than \(h\nu-\Phi\). The paper then replaces the equation by an inequality: in its letters, Π times E, plus the escape work for a gram-equivalent, is at most Rβν.
In the explanatory letters: \(eV_s\le h\nu-\Phi\). Losses can only lower the stopping potential; they cannot give one electron more than the quantum it received.

The inverse process, cathode luminescence: electrons that have fallen through a potential produce light. Reversing the budget, the energy supplied per electron must be at least the energy of the quantum produced, \(eV\ge h\nu\) in the explanatory letters.

Worked scale from the paper: in the substances Lenard examined, the cathode rays had to fall through several hundred, in some cases several thousand, volts to produce visible light, far more than the few volts one quantum of visible light needs. The paper concludes that the kinetic energy of one electron is used to produce many light quanta.
A bound is not a promise: \(eV\ge h\nu\) states what is needed in energy, not that every collision produces light.

margin.text: This modern voltage-magnitude convention does not silently replace the paper’s printed charge and potential symbols. The historical 4.3-volt check belongs to its separately identified constant and unit convention in the photoelectric laboratory. The footnote on \(P'\) leaves room for electrons bound in neutral molecules without giving that work a value; §9 applies the same one-quantum budget to freeing an electron from a gas molecule, which is ionization.
